front: Mon grand-père a septante ans.
back: My grandfather is seventy.
context: Belgium and Switzerland say 'septante' (70) instead of 'soixante-dix'.

front: Ça fait nonante-neuf euros.
back: That comes to ninety-nine euros.
context: 'Nonante' = 90 in Belgium and Switzerland, instead of 'quatre-vingt-dix'.

front: Ça coûte huitante francs.
back: It costs eighty francs.
context: 'Huitante' = 80 in the cantons of Vaud, Valais and Fribourg. Belgians say 'quatre-vingts'.

front: Voilà votre café, s'il vous plaît.
back: Here's your coffee.
context: In Belgium, 's'il vous plaît' also means 'here you are' when handing something over.

front: Viens une fois ici !
back: Come here a sec!
context: Belgian 'une fois' softens a request. The cliché is overused in jokes about Belgians.

front: Tu sais me passer le sel ?
back: Can you pass me the salt?
context: Belgium: 'savoir' is often used for 'pouvoir' (to be able).

front: On a bon ici, hein !
back: It's nice here, isn't it!
context: Belgian 'avoir bon' = to feel good, enjoy oneself.

front: Il drache depuis ce matin.
back: It's been pouring since this morning.
context: Belgian 'dracher' / 'une drache' = to pour / a downpour.

front: À tantôt !
back: See you later!
context: Belgium: 'tantôt' = later today (France: à tout à l'heure).

front: Je loue un kot à Louvain-la-Neuve.
back: I'm renting a student room in Louvain-la-Neuve.
context: 'Un kot' (from Flemish) = a student room. 'Koter' = to live in one.

front: J'ai oublié mon GSM à la maison.
pronunciation: [zhay oo-blee-ay mohn zhay-es-EM ah lah meh-ZOHN]
back: I left my mobile at home.
context: Belgium: 'un GSM' = a mobile phone. Switzerland: 'un natel'.

front: Tu peux m'envoyer un SMS sur mon natel ?
pronunciation: [tü puh mahn-vwah-yay an es-em-ES sür mohn nah-TEL]
back: Can you text my mobile?
context: Swiss French: 'un natel' = mobile phone (originally a brand name).

front: Prends un essuie pour la piscine.
back: Take a towel for the pool.
context: Belgium: 'un essuie' = a towel (France: une serviette).

front: Range tout ce brol !
back: Tidy up all this junk!
context: Belgian 'du brol' = clutter, mess (from Flemish).

front: Un cornet de frites avec une fricadelle, s'il vous plaît.
pronunciation: [an kor-NEH duh FREET ah-vek ün free-kah-DEL, seel voo PLEH]
back: A cone of fries with a fricadelle sausage, please.
context: Ordered at 'une friterie' or 'une baraque à frites'. Fries are fried twice in Belgium.

front: Je prends deux pistolets pour le petit-déjeuner.
pronunciation: [zhuh prahn duh pees-toh-LEH poor luh puh-tee-day-zhuh-NAY]
back: I'll take two bread rolls for breakfast.
context: Belgium: 'un pistolet' = a crusty bread roll.

front: Vous devez répondre endéans les huit jours.
pronunciation: [voo duh-vay ray-pohn-druh ahn-day-AHN lay wee ZHOOR]
back: You must reply within a week.
context: Belgian administrative French: 'endéans' = within.

front: Il sait tirer son plan.
back: He knows how to manage on his own.
context: Belgian: 'tirer son plan' = to cope, get by (France: se débrouiller).

front: Tu vas le faire ? – Non, peut-être !
back: Are you going to do it? – Of course I am!
context: Belgian irony: 'non, peut-être' means 'yes, obviously'.

front: Laisse une dringuelle au serveur.
back: Leave the waiter a tip.
context: Belgium: 'une dringuelle' = a tip (France: un pourboire).

front: La Belgique a trois langues officielles.
back: Belgium has three official languages.
context: Dutch, French and German. Brussels is officially bilingual.

front: Le Manneken-Pis a plus de mille costumes.
pronunciation: [luh mah-nuh-kahn-PEES ah plüs duh meel kos-TÜM]
back: The Manneken Pis has more than a thousand costumes.
context: Brussels' famous little statue is dressed up for special occasions.

front: Merci ! – Service !
back: Thanks! – You're welcome!
context: Swiss French reply to thanks, alongside 'avec plaisir'.

front: Ça joue pour toi si on se voit à huit heures ?
pronunciation: [sah ZHOO poor TWAH see ohn suh vwah ah wee TUHR]
back: Does it work for you if we meet at eight?
context: Swiss 'ça joue' = that works, OK.

front: Vous voulez un cornet ?
back: Would you like a bag?
context: Swiss: 'un cornet' = a shopping bag (France: un sac).

front: Je dois passer au bancomat.
back: I need to stop at the ATM.
context: Swiss: 'le bancomat' (France: le distributeur).

front: Passe la panosse dans la cuisine.
back: Mop the kitchen floor.
context: Swiss: 'la panosse' = a floor cloth (France: la serpillière).

front: Je me suis encoublé dans le tapis.
pronunciation: [zhuh muh swee zahn-koo-BLAY dahn luh tah-PEE]
back: I tripped over the rug.
context: Swiss: 's'encoubler' = to trip.

front: J'ai été déçu en bien.
back: I was pleasantly surprised.
context: A Swiss expression: 'disappointed in a good way'.

front: Les Suisses votent environ quatre fois par an.
pronunciation: [lay SWEES vot ahn-vee-rohn kah-truh FWAH par AHN]
back: The Swiss vote about four times a year.
context: 'Une votation' = a popular vote on a specific issue, the core of Swiss direct democracy.

front: Les Romands représentent environ un quart de la population suisse.
pronunciation: [lay roh-MAHN ruh-pray-zahnt ahn-vee-rohn an KAR duh lah poh-pü-lah-syohn SWEES]
back: French-speaking Swiss make up about a quarter of the Swiss population.
context: 'La Suisse romande' = French-speaking Switzerland.

front: Le Röstigraben sépare la Suisse romande de la Suisse alémanique.
pronunciation: [luh ruhsh-tee-GRAH-ben say-par lah swees roh-MAHND duh lah swees ah-lay-mah-NEEK]
back: The 'Röstigraben' separates French- and German-speaking Switzerland.
context: Named after the potato dish 'rösti'. Referendums often split along this line.

front: On mange une fondue moitié-moitié ?
back: Shall we have a half-and-half fondue?
context: Half Gruyère, half Vacherin fribourgeois: the Fribourg classic.

front: Tout de bon !
back: All the best!
context: A Swiss way to say goodbye and wish someone well.

front: Le français de Belgique et de Suisse n'est pas un mauvais français.
pronunciation: [luh frahn-SEH duh bel-ZHEEK ay duh SWEES neh pah zan moh-veh frahn-SEH]
back: Belgian and Swiss French aren't 'bad' French.
context: These regional forms are fully standard in their countries.
